concept.name: Call debit spread
concept.definition: A call debit spread is a vertical spread consisting of a long call at a lower strike and a short call at a higher strike, same underlying and same expiration, entered for a net debit because the lower-strike call costs more than the higher-strike call. It is synonymous with the bull call spread: a moderately bullish position with maximum gain and maximum loss both fixed at entry.
concept.intuition: You buy upside participation up to the higher strike and sell away everything above it to cut the cost — a cheaper, capped way to be bullish.
concept.mechanics: Net debit = premium paid minus premium received. Below the lower strike both calls expire worthless and the debit is lost; above the higher strike the spread is worth the strike width. The CFTC describes the call bull spread as buying the lower-strike (higher-delta) call and selling the higher-strike call, same class and expiration.
concept.formula: Max loss = net debit; max gain = (K2 - K1) - net debit; breakeven = K1 + net debit, where K1 < K2 are the call strikes.
concept.failure_modes: The capped upside lags outright calls badly in large rallies; early assignment on the short ITM leg (especially before an ex-dividend date) can leave an unintended stock position and disrupt the spread.
concept.misconceptions: It is not 'free leverage': the lower cost comes from selling the tail upside, and limited risk does not mean likely profit — the debit can still be lost in full.
concept.example: Buy the XYZ $100 call for $4.00, sell the $105 call for $1.50: net debit $2.50. Above $105 the spread is worth $5 (gain $2.50); at or below $100 the $250 debit per spread is lost.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
